speechtext: Prior to June 18, 1926. there had been a communication from the United States Secretary of State, through the British ambassador suggesting the negotiation of a treaty supplementary to the treaty of the 6th of June, 1924, providing for the refusal of clearance to shipments of merchandise from a port of either country to a port of the other country if such shipments comprised articles prohibited or restricted importation in the country of destination. These proposals were followed in April and May, 1926 by requests for a statement of opinion on the part of the Canadian government and at the date of the report of the special committee of the House of Commons negotiations for a conference on the subject were still pending. The royal commission appointed later instituted enquiries in respect of the same subject and the Canadian government expressed its willingness to hold a conference with the United States' authorities as suggested, but felt that the conference should not take place until the report of the royal commission was available. subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
When the house rose last evening at six o'clock I had just about concluded my remarks. I had dealt with several reasons why the house should support the motion of the member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner), and I was referring particularly to some of the objections raised toy the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), who stated that different provinces throughout the Dominion were objecting to having grants made by this parliament, with strings attached to them. This objection would apply to the legislation of a year or so ago when the minister was so urgent in foisting upon the provinces the old age pensions.
When I turn to the estimates and see that $100,000 is being asked to maintain an embassy at Washington, $80,000 for one in Paris and $75,000 for one in Tokyo, I cannot see how this government can refuse to grant some aid to the different provinces of Canada to build roads. There must be members on the other side of the house who dare not go back to their constituencies and say that they did not support this resolution.
The Minister of Railways said that he was convinced this matter would be taken care of some time, but the time is not ripe just now.
I wish to state again, on behalf of the people of the province of Ontario, from which I come, that I look to this government to do something to increase the happiness and prosperity of the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
If the resolution which
is before the house means nothing more than appears on its face, I see no reason why it should not be adopted unanimously. The resolution is worded as follows:
Whereas the need for establishment of national highways is greater than in 1919; rMr. Motherwell.]
And whereas in that year the Dominion government recognized its responsibility in this matter by a substantial grant, which grant is now exhausted;
Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this house the government should consider the advisability that a further federal grant be made to cover the next five years' development of highway construction.
I assume that some hon. members will attach importance to the words "should consider." If that is all the resolution is intended to imply in the way of an obligation on the government, I would say the government is prepared to assume that obligation at once. I would go further and say that the government will not only assume at once the obligation to consider, but that the government has been considering this matter for some time, is considering it now, and will continue to consider it. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, as hon. gentlemen will be quick to recognize, that if the government were to take this resolution literally, as it appears on its face, and were to act only in accordance with such an interpretation, the next thing we should hear would be that we had deceived the house, that we had not been perfectly frank with the house, that the resolution did not mean what it appears to mean on its face, but that it meant that the government was to be committed definitely to grants for highways, whether provincial highways or a national transcontinental highway.
May I say in regard to the alternative interpretation, that if the purpose of the resolution is to commit the government to making immediate grants for provincial highways, or to commit the government to immediate grants to a national transcontinental highway, the government does not feel that at the present time it is in a position to make that commitment to parliament.
In order to appreciate the significance of this resolution, I think it should be taken into consideration along with other resolutions of a similar character which are being moved by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house at the present time, and their cumulative effect considered in relation to the attitude being taken at the moment by hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to numerous other expenditures which they have been advocating or are about to advocate. Let me make clear what is quite obvious, namely, that up to the present time hon. gentlemen have been asking the government day after day to spend more money. That has been the nature of practically all the requests that have come to us thus far from the other side of the house. Up to the present moment we had not had from the other side of

If all these are taken together and if the government begins to accept them, I am afraid that after we have discharged our commitments and taken out of the federal treasury all these grants to further aid the provinces, there will be very little money left with which to discharge the obligations which the federal government itself is bound to undertake. It is very easy to speak as my hon. friend who sat down a few moments ago did, in referring to the expenditures which the government is obliged to make for legations. We are not asking the provinces to make any contribution towards these objects, because they are part of the obligation of the federal government. This parliament decided that there should be legations and, that being so, they must be maintained, and maintained out of the federal treasury. One could run on in a similar manner through the list of subjects on which we are expending money at the present time. It is easy to say that if money can be spent for one purpose that it can be spent for another. I could take the provincial list and run through the subjects for which the provinces vote money and I could find many quite as worthy as the construction of highways. What about the whole school system of the province? What about the development of the natural resources of the provinces? What about the agricultural work carried on by the provinces? Are these not worthy objects? It might be asked, why should they not in the first instance be supported out of the federal fund rather than highways? The minute one begins to run over the list, one sees, may I say it very goodnaturedly, that the attitude of hon. gentlemen supporting these grants appears to be that of wishing to make good fellows of themselves, pretty much at the expense of the public treasury, more particularly when they feel they are in the happy and secure position of not being obliged to defend their attitude or the treasury, and in the further position that if we should carry out their wishes, they can then turn round and attack us because of necessity we are obliged to tax the people a little more than we otherwise would be obliged to. We can do all these things if hon. gentlemen opposite wish them done and the rest of the house is prepared to agree with them. But we cannot do them and at the same time reduce taxation. We cannot do them and keep down expenditures, we cannot do them and proportionately reduce t'he public debt. If hon. gentlemen will realize the position they are taking, they will see it is simply this: they are asking the

National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
government to undertake obligations which will mean increased taxation to the people of Canada, which will mean an increase of expenditures in relation to receipts and a possible return to the old system which prevailed prior to the time of the present administration assuming office, of deficits instead of surpluses in the year's balancing of the public accounts.
The hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Simpson) made a specious sort of appeal yesterday. He said that the government of the day between 1919 and 1921 were able to give grants to highways, grants to technical education; that they were able to do this and to do that; and then asked, why the present administration could not do the same. I suppose we could if we washed to follow the methods of hon. gentlemen opposite, but how did they accomplish their ends? They made the appropriations they did and were able to make them by virtue of borrowing and by increasing the public debt and leaving it to their successors to pay off the debt and sundry other obligations by taxation which they would have had to raise, had it been their policy to avoid a further increase in the public debt.
Let me call to mind the old maxim that it is well to be just before we are generous, and see how far it has been followed by hon. gentlemen opposite. In the fiscal year ended 1919 there was an increase in the public debt of Canada of over $3S2,000,000.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: And all the rest. My hon. friends opposite are like the ostrich with its head in the sand; they are deliberately deceiving themselves; they will not look at the facts. At the end of the fiscal year 1921 there was a deficit of $92,000,000. Let us take the next year. In 1922 when this government had been in office only a short time we had to face at the end of the fiscal year a deficit of $81,000,000, a further increase in the public debt. When we came into office, what was the first object we undertook to accomplish? I recall very well the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, at that time Minister of Finance, telling parliament that unless we balanced the budget the country would get deeper and deeper into debt; that we were heading toward a state of national bankruptcy and that Canada's credit would be absolutely ruined throughout the world. Mr. Fielding took the position that the first thing to do was properly to balance the public accounts. There were two ways in which that could be done; one was to reduce expenditure and the other was for the time being to increase taxation, so that every year we would not be running more deeply into debt but would be placed in a position to pay off obligations which hon. gentlemen opposite had imposed upon us.

We reduced expenditures and imposed some increased taxation for the purpose, mark you, of meeting obligations which were left to us by the previous administration. At first about all that we were able to do was to hold the deficit at the point at which it had been the year before. The deficit instead of being $92,000,000 was brought down to $81,000,000 in 1922. In the following year-that is, the fiscal year ended March 31, 1923-by pursuing the policy which we had adopted we reduced the deficit to $31,000,000. From that time on instead of deficits we have had sur-

The government's desire in this matter is not in any particular to refrain from assisting every worthy object that can be assisted, but rather to recognize in the first place what our immediate obligation is, to carry on the policy
[Mr- Mackenzie King.]
which we have adopted, and which we believe will appeal more to the people of Canada than grants to provincial governments, a policy of having surpluses every year, and every year a still further reduction in taxation.
The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) suggested that we should have a national highway. The first suggestion was that we should make grants toward provincial highways, and then my hon. friend, not having much responsibility in the matter, goes a step further and suggests a national highway. If the debate runs on very much longer some hon. gentleman opposite will be suggesting an empire highway. Why, it will be asked, should we not link up the different parts of the empire with a highway? Let the motorists from Canada visit Australia and those from South Africa come to Canada, and-

Minister of Agriculture was seeking to practise the economy which my friends opposite advocate.
Where are we to end if that is to be the policy? But let us stop at the point proposed by my hon. friend from Kindersley- a national transcontinental highway. Has he any idea what such a highway would cost this country at the present time? In the first place, to be of any use it will have to be a hard-surface highway; it will have to be kept suitable for motoring in winter as well as in summer; it will have to traverse parts of this country through which, up to the present time, there has been considerable difficulty in constructing roads; it will have to be linked up by means of bridges. I am advised by expert opinion in the Department of Railways and Canals that the least amount for which we could expect to accomplish the end my hon. friend has in view is an expenditure of $200,000,000.

I want hon.
gentlemen to see what they are asking the treasury to do. That is the amount at an estimated cost of $50,000 a mile. Possibly

National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
there should be deducted from the total something for provincial highways that are already serving the purpose in part. A highway of this character, to be of any real service, would have to touch the main cities of the provinces through which it passed; nothing less would satisfy them, and that would mean a highway at 'least four thousand miles in length. I repeat, what my hon. friend is asking is that the government shall now say it is prepared to make grants to the provinces, or undertake the work immediately themselves if you wish, involving an expenditure of $200,000,000. But that outlay does not include maintenance; once the highway is constructed we will be expected to keep it in repair and in condition for use in winter as well as in summer. These are considerations of which the government has to take account, and I say to hon. gentlemen opposite, if we cannot support the resolution it is because we cannot honestly say to the country that we think this is an expenditure which the Dominion would be justified in making at this time. Undoubtedly a national transcontinental highway will come in time. It is coming by degrees already; the provinces are doing considerable work in developing highways within their owrn jurisdiction, and there is no reason to doubt that the time will come when from coast to coast there will extend a highway to serve the purposes that hon. gentlemen hope it will serve. But at the present moment we do not feel justified in leading the house or the country to believe that we are about to embark on a motor highway involving such an expenditure as I have just mentioned.
So far as the provinces are concerned, I submit that the federal government has been pretty generous in its treatment of them. To-day we are exacting much more in the way of taxation than are the provinces combined. Why should we obligate ourselves still further to increase federal taxation, while the taxation being levied by the provinces-who, after all, we are told, are going to profit most by this project-is to be left at its present rate. If the provinces wish to undertake the work- and highways come within their particular jurisdiction-they are the bodies which should increase their taxation for this purpose.
May I ask hon. members this question? Do they think the provinces would be prepared to contribute to the federal treasury for any purpose whatever? Hon. gentlemen have been saying a great deal as to what a highway will do to unite the country, how ;t will serve those who reside in the remote parts of the Dominion. Unquestionably such a
highway will be a help to some people along its route; but a service that will be much more effective in providing better communication for people who need it most is the air mail service. It will serve infinitely better to link up the whole' Dominion and to meet the needs of our people on the prairies and in remote districts indeed in a! parts of Canada.
I venture to say that if we have two hundred million dollars available for immediate expenditure, we can spend it to much greater advantage, so far as the whole of Canada is concerned, by developing air services that will carry the mails rapidly from one part of the country to another, than by constructing a single motor highway across the country.
And I venture to think that hon. gentlemen will agree that if we are to extend our trade we shall have to increase our trade commissioner service throughout the world. Will the provinces aid us, will they contribute something towards placing trade commissioners in all parts of the world, and towards the expense of collecting information on trade and markets which will be of service to the Dominion, yes, but of very special service to every province as well?
I think the house needs to appreciate that in the wisdom of those who were responsible for shaping our constitution, certain obligations were placed definitely upon the federal treasury, and certain upon the provincial treasuries. The first duty of the Dominion :s to meet the obligations which were thus placed upon it, and which will not be contributed to by the provinces.
This aid-to-highways project was started, as has been said, at a moment when the country was facing a quite exceptional condition. Our soldiers were beginning to return from overseas, and were about to be reestablished in civil life. It was recognized that as the war veterans came home it would not be possible quickly to reinstate them in their different business pursuits and avocations, and that for many something in the way of temporary employment would have to be provided, that otherwise there would be following upon their services overseas a large number of unemployed because sufficient work was not available to absorb the large number of men who were returning home. The Minister of Railways and Canals of that day, the Hon. Doctor Reid, made this very plain when he asked parliament to vote an amount towards highway construction. In the House of Commons debates for 1919. at page 3S99, Doctor Reid is reported as follows:
As I said when introducing this bill, these highways will also provide employment for the
316	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
returned soldiers. Perhaps at the present time there may not be so great a demand for employment by the returned soldiers; they perhaps do not wish to go into employment immediately upon their return home; but the time is coming when employment will have to be provided, and I think it is the duty of the government to provide employment in the way of good roads and other works of benefit to the country.
Undoubtedly the contributions did help in that way. But the government did not stop at that point in assisting the provinces to meet that exceptional condition. The government came along with grants in aid of unemployment. Despite this -particular work on highways there was a great deal of unemployment, and the federal treasury was asked to contribute to the provinces and to the municipalities in the form of unemployment relief. About all the thanks the federal treasury received was that when several millions of dollars had been contributed, the provinces turned around and said: but you have assumed this obligation, you must go on and assume it for all time to come. In addition we have had as a consequence the view expressed from the other side of the house that it is the business of the federal government to look after unemployment. As the federal government moves into the provincial field now here and now there, it simply serves to encourage the provinces to look to the Dominion to carry out their own immediate obligations. Fro-m 1920 to 1927 this government paid a total of $1,865,880 in unemployment relief in the various provinces-unemployment relief alone. And what have we done in assisting the provinces in other directions? In agricultural instruction, between 1912 and 1924, under the act that was passed to supplement the work of the provinces, we spent SI 1,399,-8S2. On technical education we have spent up to the present time 7,396,888, and we are proposing by the bill which is now before the house to contribute another $2,500,000. Under the Highways Act-the -measure which is being referred to at the present moment-we have given the provinces $18,775,604. Grants to municipalities in -relation to unemployment I have already given. To supplement the propaganda of the provinces in regard to venereal diseases we -paid out between 1918 and 1927, $1,148,237. In respect to unemployment offices which are being carried on by the provinces we spent, between 1918 and 1927, by way of supplementing their revenues from the federal treasury, $1,635,816. In other words, for the periods I have indicated, we have given to the provinces from the federal treasury under these few heads, not to mention others, a sum in excess of $42,000,000 to assist them in car-ry-

ing on work which is their -primary obligation. And in addition thereto we 'have been increasing the annual subsides it-o the -provinces. We are at this moment carrying on an inquiry in one province, and -conducting negotiations with others, which may lead to a further increase in the subsidies which we are granting and which the provinces a-re free to use for any purposes they like. To the maritime provinces, until we finally settle their claims, we have added within t-he last year o-r two annual amounts -as follows: to Nova Scotia, $875,000, to New Brunswick, $600,000, and to Prince Edward Island, $125,000.
May I direct attention to this further fact which bears immediately upon the grants from the federal treasury to the provinces. I believe that everyone who has given any attention to public finance will agree that it is a thoroughly vicious system to have one body raise taxes and another body expend the money thus secured. In other words, give to the provinces these grants from the federal treasury, without their being obliged to raise the money themselves by taxation, and you will not get, with respect to expenditure, that careful supervision which would be exercised if the provinces themselves were obliged to raise the money in the first instance. It is a bad system, a thoroughly vicious system, and that is the reason why the present administration has been seeking to put an end to a system that grew up at a time when the country was in the throes of war or had to meet a post-war situation-a system which, had it been permitted to develop, would have become thoroughly destructive of anything in the shape of economy with respect to the expenditure of the people's money.

speechtext: Why doesn't the government provide for old age pensions itself instead of shifting it to the provinces?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
It is the province's obligation, and so far as this government is concerned we have sought to safe-

National Highways-Mr. Mackenzie King
guard the public treasury to the extent at least of one half of the required expenditure whereas hon. gentlemen opposite claimed they were prepared to duplicate what we are doing by assuming the entire obligation. What has been already paid in old age pensions in the province from which my hon. friend comes? We have given to the province of British Columbia $423,105.84; to the province of Manitoba $122,332.42; and to the province of Saskatchewan $76,417.62; or a total to these three provinces, thus far, of $621,855.88. I assume that most hon. members here will live to see the day when every province in the Dominion will have an old age pensions system, and when that day comes the tax upon the federal treasury, to meet the obligation parliament has assumed, will be a much vaster sum than I have indicated. Indeed, I am told that it is estimated at an annual payment of some $12,000,000. When, therefore, we have undertaken to assist the provinces in the matter of old age pensions to the extent of $12,000,000, we can afford I think to let them in the meantime look after highways, which is their immediate obligation.
Let me come to another phase of the question. The provinces, so far as their expenditures are concerned, have been in no way affected by the very exceptional obligations which have been imposed upon the federal treasury-obligations that have grown out of the war. I challenge hon. gentlemen to point to any appreciable expenditure which the provinces have to meet to-day as a consequence of the war. The provinces have been left clear of all obligations in that direction. The Dominion has assumed a very liberal interpretation of its duty with respect to war expenditures. It has not taken, as some have contended it might have taken, the narrow view that while, with respect to defence, we were obliged to meet the actual cost- of war during the progress of war, such matters as unemployment resulting from the war, disablements, pensions, and so forth, did not constitute a federal obligation. We have never taken that attitude; we have assumed the whole responsibility. And what has that responsibility involved in the way of expenditures? To mention only the present annual expenditure attributable to the war, first of all the interest on public debt-the increase in interest, not the total interest on public debt; the annual expenditure for which the Dominion has obligated itself-is over $116,000,000. War pensions amount to $38,000,000; soldiers' civil re-establishment, $6,000.000-I am speaking now of annual expenditures which we have to face; soldiers'
land settlement administration, $1,000,000; Imperial War Graves Commission, $573,000; battlefields memorials. $183,000; adjustment of war claims, $1,656,000-or a total annual additional charge on the treasury, with respect to these obligations which we have assumed and to which the provinces have not contributed in the least particular, of $165,000,000. In the year 1928 over 454 cents out of every dollar expended by the government was attributable to the war.

speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been speaking about the laudable nature of highways, the useful purpose they serve, and so on. I should like to know whether there is a more laudable or worthy object than the one which I have just been discussing. But you do not find advocates in the provincial legislatures suggesting that because the recognition of war service is a laudable object their treasuries should be charged with the expenditures which are undertaken by the Dominion government.
Charity begins at home, and the provinces have followed that maxim pretty closely; they have looked after themselves. I challenge anyone to point to a single instance in which they have made any contribution whatever towards any object of federal expenditure. I might go a little further and say that the provinces are well able to do a little more, in regard to some of these things, than they have done. Since these grants were made in the first instance many of the provinces have discovered new means of raising revenue. I shall not mention all the provinces, but I might refer to the two which have received the largest share of federal assistance by reason of the fact that they are the largest provinces.

National Highways-Mr. Bennett
Since this system of making grants from the federal treasury to the provinces was started the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have taken over complete control of the liquor traffic and have made profits from the sale of liquor. The net profit of the province of Ontario for the last fiscal year was over $7,000,000; the net profit of the province of Quebec was over $6,000,000 and to this sum may be added a further amount of $1,451,000 from permits and seizures. If these provinces are adding to their revenues about $7,000,000 a year from the sale of liquor surely they can be expected to use at least a part of this for these highways which are so beneficial to the people. I ask my hon. friends as members of the federal parliament to apply to the provinces the arguments they have been applying to the Dominion, and to remember that their first duty is to safeguard the public treasury of this country.

Department of Education; revenue for fiscal year 1926. Ordinary; main office; federal subvention for promotion of technical education, $340,915.56.

speechtext:
I was reading from page
16, statement 6, of the public accounts of Ontario, where I find the following:
Department of Education; Revenue for fiscal year 1926: Federal subvention for promotion of technical education, $340,915.56.
That is what I find there, and when he says the government fails to discharge its obligations with respect to national highways because there is not sufficient advertising of the generosity of the parliament of Canada, it does violence to one's understanding of just what may be a sound reason.
Now let me go a step further. The constitution of this country makes provision as to how money is to be raised by taxation. Subsection 3 of section 91 provides that the Dominion parliament may raise money by any mode or system of taxation, but section 92 of the British North America Act provides that the provincial legislatures may raise their money by direct taxation within the province, for provincial purposes. In other words, a limitation is imposed upon the rights of provincial legislatures to impose taxes whereas the parliament of Canada, representing all the people and all the provinces, may raise money by any mode or system of taxation. What is to be done with the money thus raised by any mode or system of taxation is wholly within the power of this parliament to determine, and the question which must be considered by every government is how pressing are the necessities that warrant the appropriation of moneys thus raised to what the Prime Minister has called provincial objects. But, sir, he overlooks the one great fact that the same citizens pay the taxes. That is the essential thing which has been overlooked; whether you consider them as residents of a province or as residents of the Dominion the fact is that the citizens of Canada pay taxes both to the provincial and the federal treasury, and because under our constitution the Dominion may raise money by any mode or system of taxation it has the increased obligation to see to it that in the distribution of these moneys there are those compensating adjustments which place the provinces on a parity with respect to the development of the na-

National Highways-Mr. Bennett
tional policies of Canada. The Duncan report is based upon the great principle that the application of great national policies to this country has not brought equal benefit to every section of it, and therefore there must be compensating adjustments from the federal treasury to the end that every province may receive those benefits which it is intended they should have received by reason of being part of our federal union.
So much for the argument with respect to the lack of publicity or the lack of recognition of high merit on the part of this parliament in voting money to the province of Ontario for technical education. There was a statement, however, which must not be permitted to go unchallenged at this time. The Prime Minister read from the public accounts of this country, but surely he did not intend to leave the impression his remarks would leave upon parliament and the country if they were not contradicted. There are two divisions of the revenues of Canada; the consolidated fund is that fund into which all the ordinary taxes of this country are paid whether they be derived from customs and excise or from direct taxation. Into that fund is paid nearly all the moneys of this country, but when the Minister of Finance paid into it the reparations money paid by Germany to discharge the obligations of that country to our private citizens, in my judgment he did what was wholly erroneous and totally wrong. I make that remark in passing because it was a wrong act on his part to take the reparations money which, under a treaty, was available for the purpose of discharging the obligations to private citizens, put it in the consolidated fund and then go about the country saying how much he had reduced the debt of Canada by depriving people of the money to which they were entitled.
Now let us look at the consolidated fund of this country, and I would like the Prime Minister and those who sit around him to understand that when he made his observations as to the conduct of the finances of Canada during the year 1919 and later, he should have turned to page 45 of the public accounts. There he will find that in every year he mentioned there was a surplus in the consolidated fund of this country. Then what did he mean by talking about deficits? What did the Minister of Railways mean by his remarks about deficits? In 1915 there was a deficit in consolidated account of $2,449724.81, but listen to these figures as to surpluses in the years following, showing the excess of revenues over expenditures in the transaction of the ordinary business of Canada. I find that in 1916 the surplus was $41,797,111.37; in 1917 it was $84,101,950.77; in 1918 it was $82,494,639.72 and in 1919, the year with which the right hon. gentleman commenced, the surplus was $80,215,464.20. In the succeeding year the surplus was $45,902,404.80; in 1921 it was $73,268,391.39; in 1922 it was $34,391,696.36; in 1923 it was $62,321,167.91; in 1924 it was $72,024,492.47; in 1925 it was $27,942,578; in 1926 it was $60,085,026.44; in 1927 it was $79,147,603.79, and in 1928 it amounted to $86,550,021.70. This represents the excess of the revenues paid into the consolidated revenue fund of this country over the ordinary expenditures of the Dominion of Canada.
Then I turn to page 44 of the public accounts and ask myself the single question: How does the Auditor General and how does the Department of Finance say that the deficits referred to by my hon. friend were made up? At every convenient season it is the practice of hon. gentlemen opposite, from their Prime Minister down, to talk about deficits, and then when they are faced with the fact that these sums were incurred in the Great war, they offer apologies or reasons why they should not have been incurred at all, as though the war was something we should not have participated in. That is the position they take.

Let us analyze for a moment the other reasons that are given. The right hon. gentleman has seen fit to give a long statement as to the millions of money expended by the Dominion in the way of gifts to the provinces. He did not point out that under our federal union the fields of taxation between the Dominion and the provinces are sharply divided. The provinces are entitled to use direct taxation only in order to raise revenue while the Dominion can raise money by both direct and indirect taxation. Since I went to live in western Canada I have realized, and I think every hon. gentleman from that part of the country has also, that the federal government is in a very happy position in being able to raise such large amounts of money through the customs duties. These duties amounted to $152,509,000 for the ten months ending January 31, 1929, an increase of $24,000,000 over the preceding ten months. During the same period the excise duties increased $6,000,000. The provinces cannot raise money by this indirect form of taxation, and this is the form of taxation which brings in the largest revenue. The western provinces in which road building is most difficult have made as large a per capita contribution to these revenues as any other part of Canada, and they are entitled to ask this parliament for those compensating adjustments which will enable them to supplement the revenues they must raise by direct taxation by grants from the federal treasury.

My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) was the one who told the federal government that a moral responsibility attached to it to finish the work begun in 1919. It is perfectly clear that the Prime Minister, having in his own cabinet one of the horrible offenders, speaks feelingly in relation to the result of the policy on which he entered. There were those of us in the house who ventured to point out that the principle was unsound, because it was not based upon contributions being made. I happen to know the Prime Minister in days gone by asserted that the contributory system was a sound system, as he did on that evening after the motion had been made; but that does not get away from the fact that it is rather difficult to suggest that the other provinces should now adopt something that the Prime Minister of our country, the chief of our government, says is a thoroughly vicious principle. It is the first time I have ever heard a prime minister commend to the people of the country a thoroughly vicious principle and it is not quite in accord with those high ideals that usually attach to the utterances of prime ministers with respect to their commendations to the people of the country. I cannot let this pass without making the observation that we on this side of the house contend that, by the application of ordinary business acumen to the estimates of the country and the practice of that measure of economy that would be practised by men in their ordinary business, sufficient money could be saved to enable both technical education and roads to be taken care of. supporters from Saskatchewan, when they collected $152,000,000 out of their pockets by customs taxes in ten months, the highest ever taken in the history of the country. But I was so vastly interested in our empire highway. On sea and land we are now to have established, as the right hon. gentleman says, a system of imperial highways.

that community, replied, " the public be damned." and the Minister of Agriculture says, "Well, what have you got to say aibout it?"
The position of the opposition on this matter is very simple. We say that when a country raises over 8400,000,000 per annum, the largest sum that was ever raised in the history of this country, a finance minister who has a desire for economy, and a prime minister surrounded by those who desire to assist the public service-I am not going to traverse that now, for I can only speak with respect to the amendment-should be able to find a sufficient sum of money to complete a national highway in this Dominion extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, linking up the provinces, and supplying means and facilities whereby communication may be readily maintained between the various peoples of this Dominion.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I did not intend to take any part in this debate, but certain references have been made to my attitude in regard to federal grants when I was Premier of New Brunswick and at the same time president of the Good Roads Association of Canada.
I have listened with a good deal of attention to the discussion which has taken place on this resolution, but when I look at this resolution, what do I find? I find in the first place that it is not a statement of fact. If you will read the resolution you will see what I mean. It says:
Whereas the need for establishment of national highways is greater than in 1919-
Now the principle of a national highway was never laid down in the act of 1919-never. If you will read the speeches of the then Minister of Railways, Hon. Mr. Reid, you will find that he defined the purposes for which this money was to be expended, and in no case did he refer to national highways. I was at that period Minister of Public Works in the province of New Brunswick, and had considerable to do in conferences with the then federal government, with the Minister of Railways, and with his highway board, in connection with this grant. On that occasion, as on this occasion, I refused as Minister of Highways in New Brunswick to accept a grant of the federal government for highways with any strings attached to it. I refused on two grounds: First, that the standard they were setting up was too costly for the maritime provinces, too costly even for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and certainly too costly for the western provinces. The
regulations as first submitted to the conference laid down a standard of road which would cost $20,000 per mile, and the maritime provinces and the western provinces could not afford to spend money at the rate of $20,000 per mile in order to get a grant of 40 per cent of the expenditure from the federal treasury.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Do you mean that for every province?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Yes, sir. The hon. gentleman shakes his head. Allow me to tell the hon. gentleman that the regulations under the Highway Act as first submitted to the conference in 1919 laid down a standard of hard surfaced roads, and nothing was under the cost of $20,000 per mile. That was one of the reasons why I, as Minister of Public Works in the province of New Brunswick, refused to take that grant. My other reason was that if the federal government was going to give aid to highways in the provinces, they had no right to say to the provinces what kind of road they were to build. That should be left to the discretion of the provinces themselves and the money should be given without any strings attached. That is the stand I took then.
Later on, in the fall of 1919, on the 6th day of October, the federal highway board visited the maritime provinces. On behalf of the province which I then had the honour to represent I still had up to that time refused to expend any part of this federal money. We went on with our own program and our own system of aiding highway construction. In October the federal highway board, accompanied by its engineer, Mr. Dick, came to New Brunswick and the maritime provinces, and met the ministers of highways of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and New Brunswick, and after they viewed the situation as they had found it in the three maritime provinces, they consented to modifying their standard, and the result was that money was then granted to Prince Edward Island, which was building dirt roads, and to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, which were building gravel roads according to the standard then in practice in the province of New Brunswick, and I may say that the standard of gravel roads as constructed in New Brunswick under the engineers of that province, and independent of federal government, is the standard of gravel roads approved by the federal board throughout the whole length and breadth of Canada to-day. Up to that time, the 6th of October, we had refused to participate in the

National Highways-Mr. Veniot
federal grant, for the reasons I have given, but when their standard was modified, with 328 miles of main trunk roads constructed in the province of New Brunswick under the standard I have mentioned, in the month of December of that same year an order in council was passed approving of the plans, specifications and standard of gravel roads in the province of New Brunswick, and the federal government paid to us $250,000 for the work that we had done during that year.
I have stated that in the beginning I was opposed to federal aid with strings attached. It is quite true that when the other provinces accepted this federal aid, I recommended to the province of New Brunswick, as Minister of Public Works, that they should do likewise. It is quite true that in 1923 or 1924 I came to Ottawa as president of the Dominion Good Roads Association, and on their behalf and on behalf of the province I represented, I presented memorials for the continuation of the federal aid to highways. But since that date I have found myself in very good company. When I came to Ottawa as a minister in the federal government, I was still of that opinion, and when I sat in conference and listened to the provincial premiers telling the Prime Minister of this Dominion that they wanted no such grants with strings attached, but that what they waned was an increase of their subsidies, and to be allowed to do with that increase that which they thought best, I was convinced that I was in better company than I had hitherto been with the Good Roads Association because the provincial premiers in that conference were carrying out the very principle that I laid down as Minister of Public Works in New Brunswick in 1919. It is for that reason, and in order to explain my position in connection with the vote I am about to give, that I rose to speak this afternoon. I am convinced that following out the principles that were laid down by the representatives oi the different provinces of the Dominion of Canada, I can justify my vote in voting against the resolution as it is presented to this house.
Let me point out one further consideration, Mr. Speaker, Why should any hon. member propose a resolution of this kind in direct opposition to the expressed views of the premiers of the provinces in conference assembled in Ottawa? Surely those gentlemen know what they want. Surely it is not our place to say to them: We know better than you do what you want. They told us they did not want this assistance, and that is the

reason why I am justifying my vote this afternoon in opposition to the resolution as it was at first introduced.
I believe that sooner or later we may have to come to the consideration of a national highway.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Why not now?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend, I think sufficient reasons have already been advanced why we should not do so now. The arguments to which I have listened in this debate convince me that very few hon. members have any idea of what the construction of such a road will cost. In other words, they have very little idea of what has yet to be done to complete a national transcontinental highway. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has stated that he has been informed that there is no more than six hundred miles of road to be completed to bridge the existing gap. My hon. friend must have very poor judgment of what should constitute a national highway. There is not a mile of highway from Halifax on the one side to Sydney on the other, up to the boundaries of the province of Quebec, that can be accepted to-day as the standard for a transcontinental highway. I know whereof I speak. The hon. gentleman representing the county of Pictou (Mr. Cantley) was good enough to tell the house last night that I was the first Minister of Public Works in the maritime provinces to lay down the principle of road improvements. That is quite true. I do not refer to it for the purpose of personal aggrandizement, but everybody in the maritime provinces knows that "Good Roads Veniot" was the first to have money voted for the improved construction of highways in the province of New Brunswick. I wish to give credit to the hon. gentleman who preceded me in that office. He laid down the framework of a system of road improvements for the province, but, fortunately or unfortunately for the province, I do not know which, he did not last long enough in politics to put his system into effect. It fell to my lot to lay down this policy and carry it out.
Let me point out how the cost of road construction can be met better than the provinces are meeting it to-day. It is wrong to say that when in 1919 the federal government made grants to the provinces in aid of highway construction it imposed an extra obligation upon the provinces to spend so much money in order to get the benefit of those grants, and so encouraged them to adopt a

National Highways-Mr. Veniot
policy which later on they could not financially carry out. That is not true of Ontario, nor of Quebec, nor of New Brunswick. Long before the federal government had ever mooted the idea of granting federal aid, Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick had instituted a road-building policy which they were carrying out as rapidly as possible. In 1917 when New Brunswick began the reconstruction of main highways as well as secondary trunk roads out of money borrowed against the credit of the province-using money from the consolidated revenue fund to meet the expenses of its by-roads; they are considered our least important roads in comparison with the first two that I have named-we were receiving from automobile fees 838,000 a year. At that time there were only two thousand automobiles in the province. When we adopted the principle of funding the automobile fees to raise money for highway construction, the Good Roads Association at its first convention condemned the principle as not being practicable; but two years later, when New Brunswick was in a position to give a concrete example of how successfully that principle was being applied, the association at their Halifax convention passed a resolution recommending that the provinces earmark their automobile fees and borrow against that fund on a twenty-year basis to meet the capital expenditure on road construction. New Brunswick was the first province to adopt that principle. As I have said, in 1917 we received 838,000 from automobile fees; last year the provincial treasury received from that source 8725,000, and about $300,000 from its gasoline tax, representing a funding power of one million dollars. New Brunswick has borrowed one million dollars against this fund to carry on the construction of its main highways and secondary trunk roads, and with the provision for a sinking fund the loan will be repaid in a period of twenty years.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: If you concur in that principle, what would you say to the Dominion applying to the same purpose the money which it obtains through excise and other taxes levied on automobiles?

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
There is all the difference
in the world between the two cases. The province is collecting automobile fees and gasoline tax from those who use its roads, and has no right to apply that money to any other purpose than the reconstruction and upkeep of those roads. Take the province of Ontario, it receives annually from automobile fees and gasoline tax over three million
dollars. I understand the province does fund a part of this revenue for the construction of roads, but not for maintenance. Why should not a rich province like Ontario fund more, if not the whole, of its automobile fees to look after its highways? The money is collected from those who by their use of the provincial highways necessitate heavy expenditures in maintenance and reconstruction. It is a fair proposition. The owners of automobiles should pay for the upkeep of the highways because they are the ones who destroy them. Everyone knows that no matter how you construct any kind of hard surface road, or even a gravel road, there is no such thing as permanency. You cannot find, either in Canada or anywhere else in the world, material that will make a highway which you can claim to be permanent; there is always a certain maintenance cost to meet One of the best highways on the North American continent, between Montreal and Quebec-what is known as the King Edward Memorial highway-is costing the province of Quebec to-day at least from four to five thousand dollars a mile for maintenance. I have travelled over highways between here and Toronto, hard surface in some places and gravel in others; they are among the best roads I have ever travelled over in my life, and yet the upkeep is enormous. I do not see, therefore, how it can possibly be suggested that the federal government should grant money to aid in the construction of purely provincial roads,-I am not referring now to national highways. If that contention were conceded and we contributed money now to a greater extent than we have done in the past, or on as large a scale as we did in 1919, when the provinces received but little revenue from automobile fees, what would be the next step which the provinces would ask us to take in connection with responsibilities that should be theirs?
I did not intend taking up so much time, but I wanted to explain my position in regard to this resolution. From what has occurred in the last three or four years, the changed conditions and the altered opinions of the Prime Ministers of the different provinces, I am perfectly justified in assuming the position I intend to take in voting against the resolution. Before I resume my seat, however, I wish to refer to a remark made by one hon, member in discussing the resolution. It was uncalled for and I believe, had he given it sober, second thought, he would not have made the remark. We may differ with one another; one province can differ with another

National Highways-Mr. Veniot
in its aims and aspirations; in the nature of things we do differ. But when an hon. member from Ontario is so much at a loss for argument that he must condemn public expenditures in the maritime provinces as a means of saving some money to spend on the roads in Ontario, then I think his argument is very far-fetched; it is not worthy of that hon. gentleman.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that at the Dominion-provincial conference all the provinces were opposed to a federal grant for highways construction? At page 31 of the report of the conference I read that:
On the question of aid for highway construction practically all the provinces, with the exception of Quebec, favoured assistance from the federal treasury.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I thought I made myself clear. I said that they opposed the granting of federal aid to anything in connection with provincial responsibilities which had any strings attached to it; and I was all the more convinced that I should support the policy which I laid down in 1919 as Minister of Public Works in New Brunswick.
In conclusion, may I express some surprise at the heat displayed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in his reply to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). Really, to say the least, it was comical to hear the leader of the opposition preaching economy. When you look back on his own record and the record of his own party, no matter at what time they were in power, and then hear the present leader of that party stand up and preach economy, it is enough to make anyone laugh.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: A good many of them were laughing.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Why did he not preach and practise economy when he had the opportunity? Take him when he was Minister of Finance for a few short months in the shadow government. What did he do? You will find, if you examine the records, that this apostle of economy, this watchdog of the treasury, consented to the expenditure of some $55,000,000 without any authority from parliament, in order to help elect his friends in different parts of the country.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: I am sorry I must contradict the hon. gentleman. The reports brought down by the succeeding Minister of Finance indicated-

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: I thought I would bring him to his feet.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: Oh no. The reports, I say, indicated that the estimates had been followed in their entirety.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knew that between July 3 and September 14, 1926, $55,000,000 was expended without one tittle of authority from parliament; and expended where? In the very places referred to last night by his colleague from Ontario where, according to him, the construction of breakwaters and wharves was undertaken, in Quebec, and in the maritime provinces, as a sop to the Liberals. A good many ministers have been visiting Toronto and other parts of Ontario and have been telling the people how prosperous this country is; you have only to put your hand in your pocket to find gold and silver. But what is the situation? When the Laurier government came into power the country was spending $36,000,000 whereas to-day it is spending $400,000,000; yet it cannot afford a few dollars for a national system of good roads. What the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) said yesterday has a good deal of common sense in it. The city of Toronto has to spend money on. roads for a radius of fifteen miles outside the city to help the farmers bring their produce in. What this country needs is a national policy in relation to good roads. We have had the most insane railway policy of any country in the world; with useless duplication and waste as a railway policy, and the Liberal party created that debt by building the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. If one fraction of that money had been spent on good roads it would have been

National Highways-Mr. Church
much better for the country. Under the Beveridge bill of the United States the federal government grants money to the state legislatures, and the states build the roads to conform to federal standard specifications.
I congratulate the Progressives for having brought up this question; as a result of this debate the good roads movement will get into politics and it will stay in politics until the government of the day attains a proper sense of its responsibility. In the last presidential election in the United States farm relief was the great issue. Where does this government stand on the question of farm relief? The automobile and motor truck have revolutionized farm transportation, and if there is one province which gets nothing for good roads from this government it is the empire province of Ontario. The government and the municipalities of Ontario have done their duty in building good roads, receiving little or nothing from this government. The municipalities throughout the country are bearing the peak load of taxation to-day, both direct and indirect; they have not the elaborate means of revenue possessed by the Dominion, 'but to-day this government is not doing its duty in this respect. In 1896 it required 836,000,000 to maintain the country; now it requires $400,000,000, but to-day we are spending very little more on good roads than we spent in 1896. We have millions of dollars for frills and fads; $2,000,000 to date for the League of Nations, $2,500,000 for the health of animals, $100,000 for an embassy in Washington and another $100,000 for an embassy in Tokyo. If we had a proper system of going through these estimates we could eliminate perhaps one-third of them and apply the money to essentials; we could build these good roads which are so necessary to-day. I have travelled all over the province of Ontario and in many cases I find that the farmers canont get their crops to market; in the Niagara district many farmers do not gather in their fruit because they cannot get it to the cities because of the cost of transportation. Ontario has spent millions of dollars building roads even in the north, where [DOT]we had to build our own branch railway, the Temiskaming and Ontario line. Ontario wanted a subsidy from this government for the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway, which taps the richest mining district in the world to-day, but we could not get it.
The Conservative party started this good roads movement in Ontario in 1906, and the Ferguson government has done a great deal of good in this matter. Mr. Taschereau in *Quebec has done excellent work also, but nothing has been done by this federal government for the central provinces herein. I hope the farmers will take note of the fact that while this government spends money like water, no money is available for these good roads. Any municipal treasurer would strike out about one-third of these estimates, but this government is not operating in a business way. We could stop building branch lines for a year or two and devote the money to a good roads system which would be of much greater benefit. I suppose soon we will be building branch lines to the sun, the moon and the stars.
The present road-building policy of this government seems to be one which robs Peter to pay Paul. There is no such thing as equality of treatment; some provinces get something but the older provinces get nothing. We should spend $5,000,000 a year for the next ten years in the western provinces to put them on a proper footing. In Ontario, Toronto and the Ontario government built the Toronto-Hamilton highway, and now Toronto pays 40 per cent of the cost of building and maintaining it. We should have something similar to the Beveridge bill by which the federal authorities would grant money to the provinces for the next five years for the construction of roads according to standard federal specifications. If that system were inaugurated it would be a great advantage to the people of Canada. The government cannot go to sleep on this question and say they have nothing to do with the construction of good roads. The motorists of Ontario have to pay a gasoline tax, which I believe to be absolutely illegal; I think if it were taken to the privy council it would be shown that the collection of this gasoline tax by the province is ultra vires. Last year Ontario collected several millions from this tax, and a good deal of that money has been used in the ordinary business of the province instead of being devoted to good roads while also the Ontario government spent several millions on roads.
If the federal government would spend one-tenth of the money spent on useless railways we would get somewhere. East of the city of Toronto we have four roads, the Canadian National railway double tracked; we have the Canadian Pacific railway double tracked; the old Canadian Northern and Toronto and Eastern; and to-day the government are tearing up the old Mackenzie and Mann road and selling the ties and so on. That was a useless duplication and waste of money, yet we have hardly a dollar to spend on our highways. I believe if this matter were taken up by a special committee composed of all parties of the house we might formulate a national policy which would be a credit to the country.

The fact that
this resolution was introduced by an hon. member of this house is to me somewhat peculiar. We are sitting here as federal members and looking at things from the national viewpoint, and to have a resolution of this kind come before us in this way does not seem to me to be proper. Primarily this matter is one for which the provinces are responsible. It may be, as in other matters in which the provinces are primarily responsible, that this parliament might assist, but the primary responsibility rests and remains with the provinces. Surely the provinces should consider the whole question from A to Z and find out what is involved in this whole national project, and then when the matter had been thoroughly investigated you would expect the governments of all the provinces to make representations to this parliament asking for federal aid. Is that the situation here? We find that the provinces have not investigated this matter to find exactly what it means, or have not asked this parliament for any specific help. On the other hand, we find an hon. member of this house trying to say to the provinces, who have not considered the scheme, "We are going to tell you that you should have some better roads in the shape of a national highway." In my humble judgment the matter should be approached from absolutely the opposite angle.
I come from the province of Saskatchewan. It is a large province; it is a new province,

National Highways-Mr. Young (Saskatoon)
and it is sparsely populated. As far as I am concerned I want to have the best roads that we can afford, but we must consider what would be the best way to build those roads. This resolution seems to suggest that the first thing to be taken care of is a national highway from coast to coast. Such a highway would be primarily for tourists. I am in favour of bringing in all the tourists we can, no doubt about that, and if we can afford to construct all the provincial highways we need and at the same time build this national highway, I am for building both. I am told that the tourist traffic brings a large amount of money into Canada, and I believe that is true, but I want to suggest to this house, and suggest it most seriously, that the producers of grain in the western provinces bring a much larger amount of money into this great Dominion. If the farmers of western Canada were to be asked whether they wanted a national highway which would cross their province, or the class of roads which would be market roads to get them hither and thither throughout the various parts of the country, I do not believe there is any doubt as to what answer they would make. If I were a member of the legislative assembly in the province I would be obliged to consider first how I could best serve the greatest number of the people in the province. If the question of good roads arose I would have to consider as between the producers of grain and the tourists, and I am with the producers of grain always. The hon. member who introduced this resolution apparently is more concerned in getting tourist traffic travelling from one end of this country to the other than in first getting good roads for all the producers.

Another point that came up when this question was introduced into the house in 1912 was:	Should the greater be taxed to provide
facilities for the few? That is a principle we should not lose sight of when we are considering such resolutions as the one now before the house, because conditions in Canada differ in the various sections of the ocuntry. The greater part of the revenue derived by our federal exchequer is raised through the customs, and the far-away sections of the country are made to contribute according to their ability equally with the more centra! parts of the country. I think, therefore, that when we distribute federal moneys in the way the highway appropriation of $20,000,000 was distributed, the smaller provinces are placed in an unfavourable position as compared with the larger provinces to share in such a grant. My view in the past has been, and I am of the same opinion still, that it is better for the Dominion of Canada to consider the matter carefully in conference with the provinces, rather than to distribute federal monies in the way proposed in this resolution. It is better to give the provinces an increase in their subsidies, if that be necessary, to cover conditions that have grown up since the last adjustment of subsidies was made. That, it seems to me, is the fairer way. In addition, it gives the provinces the right to vote their monies for the purposes most needed in the province, whether it be the building or upkeep of roads or for some other purpose.
Dealing more particularly with the amendment that was moved by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) for a national

National Highways-Mr. Sinclair (Queens)
highway to be constructed across Canada, I just wish to say that the same argument holds good only in a more pronounced way, because the smaller provinces, and especially that province which is separated from the mainland of Canada, would not be in a position to benefit from a large expenditure of that kind in a degree comparable with the more central portions of Canada. So I feel sure that those of use who come from the eastern provinces and particularly Prince Edward Island, cannot accept the resolution of the hon. member as readily as those from the more central portions of Canada.
The expenditures that the provinces were called upon to make under the Highways Act of 1919 were met entirely by borrowings by the provinces, and in Prince Edward Island the provincial debt was doubled by the amount it was necessary to raise to take advantage of the highway grant. As has been very well stated by the hon. the Postmaster General, (Mr. Veniot), in the maritime provinces including Prince Edward Island, they did not attempt to build roads to the standard aimed at and attained in the larger provinces. In fact, they could undertake only a system of drainage of properly constructing the bridges, and of making the roads passable over the low and rough places. They did not in any degree attempt under the highway grant to surface the roads, because that would have entailed such a large expenditure in the importation of the necessary material from the other maritime provinces that it would have used up the whole grant. To extend the highway grant for another five years, therefore, would mean further heavy borrowings for the small province of Prince Edward Island, in order to put herself in a position where she could obtain the benefits extended to the other provinces.
I might add that at the time the monies were being expended the government of Prince Edward Island, in order to get the full benefit -of'the forty per cent from the federal treasury within the time that was allowed, passed an order in council expressing the view that they would not be able to earn the full amount, and asking the federal government to allow the cities of Charlottetown and Summer-.side to put up the sixty per cent and continue the highway through the cities. This was accepted by the federal government and the cities put up the sixty per cent.
I might point out that the same is true with respect to other legislation of this nature which has been passed by the Dominion government-the Technical Education Act, for instance. The matter came before the royal
commission investigating maritime claims, and the view that had been presented to the government on several occasions was again presented to the commission, which in its report recommended that a distinction be made so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned in the distribution of the funds granted by this parliament for technical education, namely, that it be extended in that province to agricultural education, as was not the case in the other provinces. It was also recommended by the commission that it be extended, if possible, to giving instruction to fishermen. So I think the house will agree with me that in passing legislation of the kind that is asked for by this resolution, the smaller provinces as well as those in the more distant parts of Canada are placed under a handicap as compared with those provinces which are more centrally located.
Further, we have no demands from the electors in our province for legislation of this kind. There is no movement among the people there for a larger grant or for a renewal of the grant of federal aid to highways. But there is a movement among our people for expenditure by the federal government in other directions, and I think it is only fair for me to interpret the wishes expressed by our people and to say that if moneys are to be expended by the federal exchequer in aid of transportation, many petitions have been circulated among the people of Prince Edward Island, by the farmers' organizations, for instance, endorsed by the boards of trade of the province as well as by the maritime board of trade at its meeting at Halifax, asking for railway extensions to different parts of the province, to serve the needs of the farming sections which are far removed from railway facilities, as well as the needs of fishing centres which are lacking in proper transportation facilities.
So I think we in the east must be guided by the wishes of the people as expressed calmly and in the light of their everyday needs, that it is better to spend federal money under the British North America Act than encroach upon the field allotted to the provinces. I would be much better satisfied to see aid given along the line that is asked for by the people of our province, rather than impose upon them expenditures that they themselves have not expressed a desire to undertake. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I shall oppose the amendment as well as the motion.

It is entirely to his credit, he is the father of those roads. In 1912, the Quebec legislature adopted a splendid measure which the people then were not very familiar with. I heard a great many fanners of various municipalities at the time the government were offering to lend them money at 3 or 2 per cent, refuse it fearing that the act might be contrary to public welfare. In 1912, the Quebec govern-
ment succeeded in negotiating a loan of more than $10,000,000 to begin the construction of gravel, macadam and asphalt roads. After this loan had been exhausted, the people then began to realize the importance of good roads. 1 personally organized delegations that called on the Quebec premier in order to request him to help certain municipalities which, after haying had doubts about the advisability of the program of good roads, wished to obtain the necessary money to build them. I heard the then prime minister tell them: "Gentlemen, this is the outcome of a good measure, when well understood. All I regret is that, in the present money market condition, it is more difficult to obtain money on such terms. I am equally well disposed and as soon as I will be able to obtain a loan on suitable terms, rest assured that I shall again be ready to listen to your requests."
We fully understand the importance of good roads in the province of Quebec. Nevertheless I think it is an excellent thing for the Dominion government to adopt a cautious policy which will permit it, from year to year, to reduce our national debt. Before we further proceed and trespass on the autonomy of the provinces, I think the government should move cautiously, as the provinces have legislated on good roads, they have spent thousands and thousands of dollars, and I am of the opinion that it would not be wise for the Dominion government, previous to studying sufficiently this measure, to agree with the motion before the house. I think that the people have no reason to be offended on the attitude taken, at present, by the government, so worthy of praise for its administration of the country's affairs. To my mind the resolution should not be adopted previous to its being sufficiently studied and before the provinces consent to shoulder their share of the burden and accept the Dominion government's invitation. Often it takes years before an important measure is carried. I was referring just now to my constituency, especially that part known in Quebec as Frontenac, whose chief town I inhabit and which I have the honour of representing, together with my colleague, the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix). In 1916, we appealed to the provincial government, as I mentioned a few moments ago, in order to obtain the building of the district road known to-day as the Victoriaville-Woburn highway and, in the direction of Beauce, St. George-Wobum highway. In 1916, we met at Megantic and discussed the important problem of district roads which later on will become international highways. Seventeen years

have since elapsed, and I wish to inform the house that in the course of the year 1930, we shall have the honour of inaugurating that highway which will link Quebec to the state of Maine extending as far as Portland.

Mr. LETEULIER DE ST. JUST:	Mr. Speaker, when the house nose at six o'clock, I was just on the point of discussing the importance of having tourists in Canada. It is certainly due to the development and improvement of our highways that such a large number of tourists have visited not only the province in which I reside, but all the provinces of Canada.
If we glance over the statement of the Bank of Montreal, for the month of July, 1928, we note that thanks to the continuous flow of American and other foreign tourists, although the latter in smaller numbers, the retail trade as a whole, improved considerably during the summer season. It is also seen in the same statement that the money spent by tourists amounted to $250,000,000. Indeed, this is a colossal figure! It is of great import that the various provinces use discretion, they must endeavour to improve their roads throughout their respective territories. However, if we examine the various aspects of the question; if we consider how our railways fare in this matter, both the Canadian Pacific and the National railways-owing to the development of good roads and the heavy traffic of vehicles of all kinds: motor trucks, motor-bus and other motor cars, during the summer season, and this is an appreciable advantage for those who love to travel through our provinces-we are aware that it is very detrimental to our railway companies, owing to the fact that they are obliged to reduce the number of trains, and, if we do not show foresight, it will become difficult to regulate the passenger service as it should be.
For these various reasons, I think we should seriously study the measure at present under consideration, both as regards the viewpoint of railways and the administration of the country.
We are all aware that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has a great responsibility towards this country. Often we hear it said that a member's burden is heavy; however, if we stop to think for a moment and consider the enormous responsibility which weighs on the Minister of Finance who is the barometer of the country's finances, there
is need to look carefully into this resolution, in order to avoid the disaster which might befall us should we become too inconsistent The economic stability of a country-we all know-begins with the good management of municipalities which make up the provinces as well as the good administration of the latter themselves, and, through this medium, the federal government is assured of being able to suitably administer our affairs, and each year report a surplus instead of a deficit.
We have been fortunate enough to witness heretofore, an ever increasing trade throughout the country. This allows the Minister of Finance and his colleagues in the cabinet to announce in the budget, each year, a reduction in taxation as well as a decrease of the national debt.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that this resolution should be withdrawn, otherwise I shall be forced to vote against it for the numerous reasons I have enumerated. It often occurs that we do not give sufficient time to questions submitted to us. However, it is true that either the permanent or special committees of this house closely examine these questions, which affords us some guarantee. Thus we have a sound federal administration, one that the people of Canada will appreciate, not only in the course of this year but in future years.
