speechtext:
I hope my words in this debate will be very few, but I am driven to my feet because of an erroneous impression which, I believe, has characterized this debate from its very beginning. It started when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) said, as reported at page 232 of Hansard:
The constitution determines what are properly federal obligations and what are properly provincial obligations. Until we have reduced the debt further and have been able to reduce the taxes upon the people, it seems to me that this matter might very well stand. For that reason I shall vote against the motion.
That was followed, in about the same strain and to the same effect, by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), who announced that he would vote against the motion. The implication, the plain implication, in the language of the Minister of Finance was that what was asked by this resolution fell properly within the province's authority and should be a charge upon the taxation which the province might impose. That is altogether incorrect. Further, the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young), who spoke but a few minutes ago, stated that this was a matter in which the provinces should get together and should determine what ought to be done, and then
334	COMMONS
National Highways-Mr. Ryckman
ask the Dominion government to act. Anyone who reads the British North America Act will feel that such a statement as that is almost foolish.
Four months ago I listened in the supreme court to an argument wherein it was said by counsel for this government that he was instructed' by the Attorney General that, where there was any matter that referred not only to national interests but to interests between two provinces, immediately the subject matter fell within the control of the Dominion. I am not supporting that argument, but I am saying that this resolution as originally placed upon the order paper stated that it dealt with a national highway, and therefore that is a subject wholly within the competence of this parliament. Even if the matter were interprovincial it would be within the competence of this parliament, contrary to the impression left by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Letellier) as I followed him. Even the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) said he regretted that the British North America Act, passed over sixty years ago, had not made provision for this particular case; he said that could not be, of course, because at that time there were no motor vehicles. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is absolutely declared by the British North America Act that this matter of a national highway or of interprovincial highway communication falls strictly within the terms of the act, so it was quite amusing to hear the Prime Minister state at least twice that this was peculiarly a question for the provinces. I deny that statement; I say it is particularly a question for the Dominion. In this connection I would refer to sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act and particularly lo subsection 10 of section 92, which specifies the subjects which come within the peculiar jurisdiction of the provinces, as follows:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:-
a. Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province.
In order to make this more emphatic, subsection 29 of section 91 states that within the peculiar jurisdiction of the Dominion, contrary to what the Prime Minister led the house to believe this afternoon, fall all such classes of subjects as are expressly excepted in the enumeration of the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces. So according to these two sections the jurisdiction of the Dominion i3 absolute in regard to communication be-
TMr. Rvckman.]
tween one province and another or several provinces. This matter of a national highway is one with which the Dominion must deal; if a province attempted to do so in collaboration with another province the objection would be taken at once that the matter fell within the jurisdiction of the Dominion.
Do not let anyone go away with the idea that the provinces should collaborate in this way or that there is any matter in relation to this resolution, either as it originally appeared or as it has been amended, which comes within the jurisdiction of the provinces. If it is beneficial to have a national highway; if it is desirable to have an interprovincial highway of this kind this parliament must decide what should be done. From what has fallen from the lips of members on the other side of the house I think it is generally agreed that, if we did not have to pay for it, it would be in the general interests of Canada to have such a highway. Other hon. members of this house have pointed out more strongly than I can hope to do the benefits which would accrue from such a highway. A short time ago in Toronto I had the pleasure of listening to an address delivered by Sir Henry Thornton before the Canadian Institute of Industrial Traffic Men on the subject of "How to sell Canada to the world." How are we to popularize Canada? How are we to get people looking towards Canada and to get settlers for our country? I do not know any better way than by showing them the goods, and I know of no better way of displaying the goods than by bringing the people here to see what Canada is and has to offer.
We were told by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) that as far as he is concerned he stands for the farmer against the tourist. So do I, but I stand for the farmer and also for the golden-egg-laying tourist, and no one should know better than the Minister of Finance what those tourists mean to Canada. How often have we heard the Prime Minister tell us that the legislation brought in by this government is intended to favour the four great basic industries of Canada? I say, Mr. Speaker, that I know of no better way to advance the interests of the farmer, the miner, the lumberman and even the fisherman than by a national highway which will bring us the golden eggs of the tourist traffic.
A rather cheap gibe, if I may use the term, was oast upon members of parliament by the Minister of Finance, although I do not believe he was referring to members on this side of the house; he must have been prompted by his experience with his own party. He said

National Highways-Mr. Ryckman
that at the beginning of the session demands rolled in upon him for subventions and aids of one kind or another, but that at the close of the session the members on this side of the house were unanimous in condemning the government for its extravagance. During this session, and any other session I may be able to attend, I purpose supporting a national highway for Canada. I have no interest but that of the Dominion; I am not aligned with those who have been described as preferring the provinces as against the Dominion. That will be my course throughout this parliament. And my course throughout this parliament, and any other I have the privilege of attending, will be to condemn the government for its obvious extravagance. Why? In the special matter that is before us we have the opportunity of expending money-I believe it would be very little if the government got together and tried to solve this problem-in a wise way, and a wise expenditure is the soundest and truest economy. This government can spend the money and get it back tenfold if they will only listen to this resolution and the amendment.
I have been interested in listening to the efforts that have been made to defeat this resolution. One argument put forward by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) was to the effect that we had $2,000,000,000 invested in railways and we should be careful in the building of good roads because we might interfere with the receipts of those railways. How futile an argument of that kind must seem to anyone supposed to know as much as the Minister of Railways should know. Documentary evidence can be found that the automobile industry has brought more actual net cash income to the railways than has been taken away by any short-haul trips made by motor vehicles in carrying either passengers or freight.
If you want to build up a country, build up its industries. The Minister of Railways referred to one case which comes closest to supporting his theory, although it is still a long way off, and mentioned Great Britain. Great Britain is preeminently a short-haul country, but what have the railways been doing there? The railways of Great Britain had been paying exorbitant dividends, and it was found that money could be saved by the use of motor vehicles. The railways have tried to meet that situation by competing with automobile traffic, and they find that they can still pay dividends although, not as large as were previously paid. Who on the other sidp will say that that result is not a good thing
for that country? I do not believe the prosperity of our railways would in any way be adversely affected should this resolution
pass.
The government, instead of being at outs with the provinces, should enter into consultation with them, with the idea of using any stretches of road that could be used-should make up their minds that they were going to bridge the gaps, whether they be six hundred or a thousand miles-we should have throughout Canada the best highway we can possibly get. Show Canada to the Americans. I would take half the money-I am speaking at random-that is given to the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) and I would spend that on national highway construction. I would bring the American people over here and show them what a desirable country we have. I am sure we would get settlers, settlers with money, the class we desire to get, people who would populate this country and become Canadians. In that way the prosperity of Canada would be upbuilt.
No one can justify his vote on this question on the ground that this graot is peculiarly a matter for the provinces, notwithstanding what the right hon. the Prime Minister has said. It is not a maitteT for the provinces; it is a matter for the Dominion of Canada. That being so, why cannot the government go right ahead and solve this problem on a business basis? It would not cost the country too much money, and we could effect the result which all of us desire.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that if the government and its supporters oppose this vote, the fact will be made widely known. I do not think the Prime Minister will take much advice from me, but I will tell him that I cannot conceive of any matter which has been before this house, certainly not at this session, which would reflect more strongly against the government than a decision that this resolution, asking that the government take this matter into consideration, should not carry.

Prior to confederation the provinces collected their revenues mainly from customs and excise duties. When confederation was proposed, the question very naturally arose: What will be the source of our revenue? The Dominion proposed to take over the customs and excise and we shall get no revenue from that source. It was understood and agreed at that time that the Dominion government would make use of certain lines of taxation and the provinces of certain other lines. But it was agreed that the Dominion, in view of what the provinces were giving up in connection with such taxes as customs and excise, should pay the provinces an annual subsidy.
I believe the subsidy which was thought to be fair and reasonable in 1867 amounted to about 20 or 25 per cent of the total revenue of the Dominion of Canada at that time. There is no doubt that expenses have grown enormously in the Dominion, and some of them very properly so. There is equally no doubt that expenditures have grown, and grown legitimately, in the various provinces. The point I wish to impress upon the house is this, that at confederation it was thought to be a fair proposition to hand over to the provinces about twenty or twenty-five ^ per cent of the total revenues of the Dominion; that was done by way of subsidy. Although I have not figured it out, I venture the statement that if that was considered a good principle to work on at that time, I do not believe that the provinces are receiving by way of subsidy from the Dominion to-day, in lieu of all that they have given up-the right to certain kinds of taxation and so forth- three per cent of the revenues of this Dominion.	.
It has been said that you may judge the progress of a country by its transportation facilities. In the old days, long before automobiles came into use, there were two mam m'eiams of tmanisipoirta.tion, the railway and the canal. The resolution asks the government to give consideration to the advisability of constructing a highway across Canadla. I should like to be able to assume that those who used that argument were sincere in doing so, but I cannot believe that, because the members [Mr. J. W. Edwards. 3
of thie government who have advanced that argument are the very persons who have violated that principle in passing the old age pension act; about that there is no question.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that this discussion will keep in the foreground a project which is of national importance. There is no doubt that there are but few members of this house who do not realize the tremendous importance to Canada of the -building of a national highway. We have been told by some of the previous speakers of the great benefits that a national highway would confer upon the Dominion, and one of the arguments is that the tourist traffic has brought 8276,000,000 into Canada, which amount, it is said, would be greatly increased did we have a national highway. There is also a good deal to be said with respect to the argument that the construction of a national highway would be the means of bringing closer together the people of the east and our Canadians in the west. I am therefore in favour of the principle of a national highway.
But, Mr. Speaker, I must differ with some of our friends on the opposite side on the question of granting subsidies to the provinces for the building of highways. My objection will be obvious to Ontario members who know the situation in northern Ontario. 
They are aware that north of the Severn river the construction of roads is under the control of the Northern Development Company, and that the money is spent to the satisfaction of the member, provided he is a supporter of the government. There is one reason why I maintain that any project for the construction of a national highway should first be fully considered and all its phases carefully studied. I happen to reside at the front door, so to speak, of the great gap which separates the east from the west and which has so often been referred to as the obstacle in the way of closer communication between the two extremes in Canada. If my hon. friends opposite who advocate the immediate construction of a national highway will stop to think, they will realize that from the city of Sudbury to the boundary of Manitoba there is a stretch of 700 miles of very sparsely settled country; indeed, between Sudbury and Fort William there are but very few residents except at divisional points on the Canadian Pacific. But this great barren area, which has frequently caused visitors to Canada to form a very wrong impression of the vast possibilities of that section of the province, has been declared, by one of those best fitted to pronounce judgment, to contain a greater amount of potential wealth than any other area of its size in the world. And the recent discoveries that have been made and that are being made almost daily lead us to believe that the area in question, this great gap sometimes called the Hump, will in the near future be a source of as considerable wealth as any other part of the Dominion. We believe that in the course of the next ten years we shall have in that section of Canada one of the largest and most prosperous mining areas in the world. This section of Ontario is one which will have to be traversed by the international highway. But anyone familiar with the situation must realize very well that over this territory covering some 700 miles, sparsely settled, where we have practically six months of intensely cold weather, such a highway will cost a tremendous amount of money and will be of use only to tourists travelling east and west. So that before any such undertaking is contemplated by any government we shall have to wait until this development has taken place which we foresee in the near future. It will then be time to determine where this highway shall be located. Is there any member of this house who would propose at the present time to construct a national highway from Cochrane to the boundary of Manitoba? Has anyone considered what the cost of main-

National Highways-Mr. Pouliot
tenance would be of a road from Sudbury to Fort William? These are factors that enter into the discussion, and I am prepared to accept the declaration of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), that in time we shall evolve a system which will provide us with a national highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

But since then things have changed a lot. In the province of Quebec some very important roads are under the entire control of the provincial government and the municipalities have nothing .to pay for their upkeep. It is a considerable improvement, on which my friend the Minister of Roads of Quebec, the Hon. Mr. Perron, is to be warmly congratulated. This is a burden which has been taken off the shoulders of the municipalities of the province of Quebec, and I hope that the other provinces will follow that very good example.
There is another matter to which I should refer; it is this: in the upkeep of roads a great improvement has been achieved from the profits derived from the sale of liquor in the provinces. A few years ago the province of Quebec started the practice of having liquor sold by the province instead of by private individuals, and, with the exception of the two provinces of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, liquor is now sold by all provincial governments. These provinces derive a substantial profit from this sale, which profit is applied to provincial expenditures and especially to education and the construction of good roads. This is the practice in Quebec under the direction of Mr. Perron, the very able Minister of Roads.
Here is the point: Is this federal government to nurse every new movement in the provinces? Are we to have a minister of highways at Ottawa and a minister for everything else belonging to the provinces? I think the idea is absurd, and I do not think the rights of the provinces should be interfered with by any action of this government.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I believe this matter belongs exclusively to the provinces
Quebec has led the way and I think the other provinces should follow. Now that the different (provinces are getting substantial profits from new sources of income I think it should be quite easy for them to look after the improvement and upkeep of roadls. The amendment states that we should construct as expeditiously as possible an all-Canadian highway from coast to coast, and I think it would be very undesirable to have this house pass that amendment to-night. The good old Book says that no man buildeth a house without first considering the cost, and I think it would be extremely unwise for us to instruct the government to build a national highway with federal funds without first knowing anything about the cost or the conditions under which it would be built. I am quite in sympathy with a national highway, and I think the government would be well advised to look into the matter seriously and without the usual political platitudes, but I am afraid I cannot support the amendment.
I am sorry that this appears to have become a party question. One of the leading Liberal papers in the province of Alberta contained a very timely editorial yesterday in which it said it was glad to see that on several questions in this house party politics had been abandoned, and for that reason men were able to speak as they thought and vote as they felt without any party club being held over them. The conclusion was drawn that the country at large was thereby much better off. I fully agree with that idea, and I think it would be a very good thing to give our attention to the merits of these questions irrespective of how they may affect the different parties.
With regard to the resolution moved by the hon member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellneri, I do not see why the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should endeavour to place a construction upon it which is not embodied in the resolution itself. I could very well vote in favour of the suggestion that the Dominion government should consider the advisability of such a highway, and I think that is what was meant by the hon. member. When the Prime Minister endeavoured to lead the house to think that by voting for the resolution we were committing the government to some expenditure, I rather differed

National Highways-Mr. Lacombe
with him; I do not think it quite right to read into a resolution something not intended to be there. Let us take the words as they are and put our own construction upon them.
However, there is a further point to be considered; I believe the resolution itself is contradictory :	It says:
Whereas the need for establishment of national highways is greater than in 1919;
That is true; that need increases yearly, but the next statement is not correct:
And whereas in that year the Dominion government recognized its responsibility in this matter by a substantial grant, which grant is now exhausted.
If I know anything about that grant it was not given for the construction of national highways. When that money was given the provincial government of Alberta they did not attempt to build a national highway; it was not in the minds of the provincial department or the people that the money was so intended. If that were the intention we have erred; the Dominion government inspectors have erred and should be brought to task, because almost all the new roads in Alberta were built from north to south rather than from east to west. There were certain conditions attached to the granting of this money, and these conditions being fulfilled the government built the roads north and south, first to Calgary and then to the boundary line. It was a highway grant and did not in any way commit the Dominion government to a national highway.

It seems to me that is
begging the question. The general interpretation placed upon a national highway is that expressed in the amendment of the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael), a highway from coast to coast. In one sense of the word it might be said that every act passed by this house is more or less of a national character by its effect and reaction, but I do not think it a fair interpretation to say that every highway built by a municipality or a province is a national highway.
I have said that the Dominion government was not committed to a national highway project by the grant of 1919. I think in consideration of these facts and in consideration of the rather ambiguous wording of the resolution in that it wrongly states that the Dominion government is committed to a national highway, I cannot support either the resolution or the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, pre-

vious to disposing of the present motion, I think that this parliament should first consider the opportunity of putting in order its own house before helping our neighbours. In fact, we have large yearly obligations which our budget shows amount to $391,000,000. Our national debt still amounts to $2,400,000,000, notwithstanding the wise administration of the present government. I therefore think it would be adding too heavy a burden on the shoulders of the Canadian ratepayers were we to undertake new obligations. It would also be, in my humble opinion, an attempt against the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces. The provinces should legislate in regard to good roads and not the Dominion government, the former collect from the ratepayers the tax on gasoline, and motor-vehicle licenses. They should therefore build and bare the upkeep themselves of their roads. Let me point out, as an example, to this house the large and beautiful province of Quebec whose magnificent national road system is the envy of all tourists who visit us during the summer season. Let me further add a word of praise with reference to a distinguished ex-premier of Quebec, the Hon. Sir Lomer Gouin, who inaugurated that truly progressive policy of our good roads. Let me also recall the truly patriotic attitude of his successor, the Hon.
L.	A. Taschereau, who still carires on that good and sound policy. Finally I wish to particularly mention the Hon. Mr. Perron, Minister of Provincial Highways. It is due to his care, foresight and energy that our national highways are an object of pride to the good old province of Quebec. The Quebec minister of roads intends to further spend $17,000,000 this year. Therefore, I am of the same opinion as the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) who certainly delivered a remarkable speech in this house, and I think that each province should follow the example of ours and that we should not apply to the Dominion government to build our national highways.
A short while ago, I heard the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) trying to compare the object of the present motion with the Old Age Pensions Act. I think that this comparison has no foundation in fact since, at present, each province has its legislation on the building of good roads while the Old Age Pensions Act has not yet been adopted by ailll the provinces. I say, sir, that the question is an entirely different one and I humbly ask the house to consider on its merits.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for all these reasons and many others which have been so forcibly and well put before this house by members who have preceded me, I shall be obliged to

National Hiyhways-Mr. Dionne
vote against the present motion if the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) insists on a vote.
Mr. GEORGES L. DIONNE (Matane) (Translation):	Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of taking part in the present debate, but seeing how it has broadened out, I think it is my duty to make a few remarks. First,
I wish to state that I shall make use of my maternal tongue and not of Shakespeare's language because it is not only our right but our privilege. Should anyone find fault, I will simply tell him "Honi soit que mal y pense."
Now, sir, I can well imagine a highway not only laid out or projected, but opened to traffic from a point on the Pacific coast, crossing every province of Canada and reaching a point on the Atlantic coast. I can imagine the splendid vista, the beautiful plains it would cross; I can visualize lofty mounts, splendid chains of mountains, vast forests and magnificent waterways strewn along its route. I realize also the pleasure felt by the tourist following this highway through a country replete with so varied and splendid panorama. However, on the other hand, I consider that the necessary expenditure for the construction of such an extensive road and the realization of such a scheme would be enormous, notwithstanding all the pleasure and advantages which would accrue to those who could afford the luxury of such a trip undertaken at various times. Let me say, sir, that the conception of such a highway was a happy one. I shall not take up the constitutional aspect of the question, it was discussed by experts. I shall neither search the British North America Act to find out 'whether the Dominion parliament should interfere in this business of building and opening up a highway, however, I shall abide by what has been done, for in Quebec this matter is closely looked after by the provincial legislature and we must add to the credit of our province that numerous, wide and well built roads that cross it in every direction, and that United States tourists or those of our other provinces, who have the opportunity of motoring over them, find that we have splendid and well paved roads and very interesting spots to visit.
I do not wish, sir, to further delay the house as this question has been sufficiently discussed. In closing my remarks I must take into consideration the views of those who will be called upon to pay the enormous amount necessary to build this highway and the large sums which he will be asked for its maintenance. Under these circumstances, I state that our financial situation does not allow us to grant subsidies for such undertakings. Therefore, I shall deem it my duty to vote against the motion of the hon. member for Athabaska.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal briefly with the subject matter of the debate before-

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext: The horn, member (Mr. Kellner) has the floor.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FEDERAL GRANT IN AID OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
When I moved this resolution, Mr. Speaker, I did not exipeot that it would give rise to such a long or so interesting a debate. I am a little amused at the tactics adopted, by the government and their supporters. We have discussed this motion more or less regularly for two days, during which time throe of the ministers made very short speeches but the rest of them remained mute. However, this afternoon some inspiration seemed to have taken bold of the party and they came out and gave us expressions of their opinions.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) complains about the members in opposition to the government and the independent members moving resolutions early in the session involving large expenditures, and then coming back later and moving resolutions condemning the government for making large expenditures. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is precisely what we are here for. If we have not the privilege of criticizing expenditures or, on the other hand, offering suggestions to the government as to where the public money should be spent, I fail to see where wie would be doing any good by being present in this house. The government have sufficient support on their benches to put through any measures they want to, and unquestionably if we have not the privilege of criticizing them we are of no use here.
When I introduced this resolution I pointed out to the house that it came to me from the United Farmers of Alberta; that many members on both sidies of the bouse bad spoken in favour of it; that I had received quite a number of letters and telegrams from private individuals recommending it, and that a few days before I introduced it the hotelkeepers' association had sent me a resolution in favour of it. When the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) spoke on this question he mentioned the hotelkeepers' association, but left out aill reference to any other association; the right ban. the Prime Minister did the same thing this afternoon. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the only reason they did that was to create a reflection against that organization, which would also include myself. I have no

National Highways-Mr. Kellner
hesitation in saying that in my bumble opinion I would 'be in just as high company with that organization, os I would be with the Liberal party.
There are many members supporting the Liberal government to-night who have spoken in favour of just such an expenditure as this. In fact, the government do not know whether or not they are in favour of it. The Prime Minister stated that if the resolution means what it sas^, the government would adopt it; I say to him that it says what it means. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) says that it & unconstitutional, and the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) is opposed to it. Where does the government stand? The Minister of Railways and Canals says it is unconstitutional, and in proof of that he submits -the statement that when the debate was in progress in 1919 some Liberal members from the west said so. That is not sufficient authority; personally I would not accept that as a very high authority and I do not think the people ait torge will do so.
A good deal of discussion has developed as to whether we are to have a national highway or whether we are to assist the various provincial governments. My contention is that under the resolution either method can be adopted, and I do not believe that the time to decide that question is during this debate. The logical course to follow would be to make a definite declaration as to whether or not we are in favour of giving any assistance and if we are in favour of giving assistance, when the legislation, if the assistance be provided in that way, is brought before the house, the house would then determine what action should be taken.
I want to make one statement in regard to a criticism which has been offered with respect to assisting provincial governments. Practically all the road building machinery that is in Canada to-day is owned by provincial governments and practically al the men who are constructing highways to-day are in the employ o-f provincial governments. It seems to me that it would be very desirable to make use oif that machinery which is now being used by the provincial governments. Of course, as the Prime Minister says, it is one government voting the money and another spending it. They are not spending it without some supervision. Unquestionably all the money that was spent under the 1919 legislation was supervised by the federal government and their engineers approved it all. I presume a similar method could be followed upon this occasion.
It has been stated that the house should not pass legislation with a string to it, and 
that was one point on which the Minister of Railways waxed quite eloquent. He even went so far as to say that when we took this money to the provincial governments they did not want to accept it. I imagine, if he had been as picturesque as he sometimes is, he would have told us that they wrapped it up in a nice little parcel and begged the pro-*vincial governments to take it, and for three or four years some of them refused. But he did not tell us why they refused. The legislation provided that 40 per cent would be spent by the federal government and 60 per cent by the provincial government, and the regulations provided that the provincial government would be at the bottom, and the federal government would be on top. It is therefore not surprising that the provincial governments would have to do their part first and I think beyond the shadow of a doubt the provincial governments would have to re-fuse to take the money until they had their roadbed ready. Saskatchewan was probably the last province to take the money under this grant. I do not think they received any of it until 1923 and possibly until 1924. The reason was this and no other, that that province did not have a mile of road on which they were justified in making application for assistance until the time they made the application.
While we are discussing the matter of having nothing to do with the provincial governments, I should like to make reference to a question that was asked in the house on February 27 of last year. The hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling) asked this question:
Did the federal government or any department thereof, enter into any agreement with the government of British Columbia, during the year 1927, for the survey of the road between Revelstoke and Golden in British Columbia? If not, has an agreement for such a survey in the present year been arranged for?
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) replied:
The subject is under discussion.
It is all right for the ministers to argue that we should have nothing to do with the provincial governments, but evidently they have changed their opinion since last year because then, according to the statement of the Minister of the Interior, they did have undertakings with the British Columbia government. I wonder whether the incentive has changed since then, whether that government is entitled to more consideration than some of the others.
I might quote many hon. members who have spoken in the house in favour of this

National Highways-Mr. Allan
matter. The hon. member (Mr. Gardiner), who leads the group to which I belong, discussing this matter last year, spoke in favour of it. He said that in his opinion the grant should be renewed. I will not read his words. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) also spoke in favour of it. He said:
I believe an appropriation such as was made in 1919 is within reason and would assist materially in regard to highways.
And he recommended that it be passed. The hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Lovie) made almost the same statement. He said:
As the provincial governments of the prairie provinces are embarking upon quite an extensive programme of highway construction, something which is long overdue, I would ask the Dominion authorities to vote this session a substantial sum of money to be paid over to the different provinces.
I might quote many more hon. members who from time to time have asked that this work be proceeded with. To argue in the house that this is not constitutional; that you are voting against it because you do not favour the method that is asked for in the resolution, is not dealing with the question in an honest and intelligent manner. Parliament should be in favour of some assistance, or it should be opposed to it, and it should be the duty and privilege of hon. members to vote on that issue without any attempt to draw this red herring across the trail. The resolution does not state in which way the expenditure is to be made. That is something that could be left to the house to decide at a later date. As regards the statement that it is unconstitutional, the government could do anything they saw fit with the money, provided, of course, they have a majority behind them, as they always have. They could even pass legislation to give it to the Minister of Railways or one of the other members of the cabinet, and that would be constitutional. I do not think there is a question in the world that that is a view which is not seriously advocated by those who are supporting the government.
An hon. member asked how we could face our constituents after having asked the government to get behind this resolution. Why do not those hon. members who were out west weeping tears of sympathy on the shoulders of the poor farmer support this resolution and help construct a highway such as it asks for, leaving the provincial governments to take care of the backwoods farmers that they are so solicitous about?
There is a clear-cut question before the house, one that resolves itself into something really worth while for Canada. There
is an opportunity to-night either to take the initial step in bringing such a constructive program into effect, or to kill it entirely. I have not the slightest doubt that there are hon. members who-intend to crucify it, and possibly that decision has been arrived at not by themselves as a matter of individual opinion, but in some little conference which has taken place outside of this chamber. I think that is the intention, beyond, a doubt. But in closing let me ask them to explain the matter fairly when they go before their constituents. There is little to be gained by trying to becloud the issue, by arguing that you are in favour of road construction, but that you do not favour the particular brand the resolution calls for, and therefore you are going to vote against it-with the result, I presume, that you will have no policy whatever.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that much has been said in the course of this debate which will impress upon the people of Canada not only the importance but the desirability of the construction of a transcontinental or national highway. I am in perfect sympathy with the principle of the construction of a national highway, not only as facilitating the means of intercommunication, but as promoting a clearer understanding and a closer relationship among the citizens of this great country. But while many things are desirable in connection with the development of this country, it does seem to me that they are not always at the moment economically practicable, and in my humble opinion the immediate and pressing need of the people of this Dominion is the construction of roads in our rural districts to facilitate the marketing of the products raised in our great agricultural areas.
The resolution calls upon the government to make grants for the construction of a national highway, which would indicate, as I think is quite apparent to every member of the house, that the provinces would also be called upon to contribute their fair share. In view of the commitments already made by this government in connection with our transportation facilities, in view of the insistent demand throughout our rural districts for the construction of roads, and in view of the extensive program of road building being carried on by our provinces to-day, to which the municipalities are called upon to contribute, I feel that our people are taxed the limit and I am obliged to associate myself with many members of the house who are opposed to this resolution at the present time.
